title: An internal debate, not a later break
body: Justin says he and many others expect a thousand years in rebuilt Jerusalem, and also that many who belong to the pure faith think otherwise. Irenaeus refuses to allegorize those promises into celestial blessings. Dionysius of Alexandria examines Nepos' temporal earthly reign and will not read Revelation by the bald literal sense. Lactantius and Commodian still narrate a thousand-year reign. That is an ante-Nicene argument, not an Augustine-only rupture.

title: How far a second repentance goes
body: Hermas and Tertullian On Repentance grant a further, narrow repentance after baptism, with public confession. Cyprian fights a cheap peace that restores the lapsed before confession and the priest's hand. The split is pastoral and internal: how mercy is given, not whether sin after baptism exists.

title: Order gathers around one bishop
body: The Didache has the assembly appoint bishops and deacons beside prophets and teachers. Ignatius already refuses church action without the one bishop, with presbyters and deacons around him. Clement of Rome traces orderly appointment from the apostles. That is development inside the same centuries, not a post-Nicene invention.

title: Pray for Caesar; refuse his gods
body: Tertullian's Apology prays for princes and will not make Caesar Lord in God's place. His Crown of the Soldier then treats the camp laurel as idolatry. Loyalty with a limit is the pattern in this library — not quietism, and not a later theory of throne and altar.

title: Call, refusal, and Origen's end
body: Irenaeus: God gave the good; those who do not work it are judged because they could have. Origen against Celsus: each still chooses, yet he also says the whole rational nature will one day come under the Word and evil be removed. That is an internal ante-Nicene tension, not a medieval add-on.

title: Thanksgiving, flesh language, one table
body: Didache gives thanks over cup and bread as a pure sacrifice of the gathered church. Ignatius, Justin, and Irenaeus say the food is the flesh and blood of the one who suffered. The library does not yet stage a later scholastic fight; it does show realism against those who abstain because they deny the flesh.

title: One God, worshiped without temples — yet with fasting and thanksgiving
body: Writers here from Minucius through Lactantius agree that one God alone is owed worship, and that the worship is a pure mind, innocence, and justice rather than temples, images, or bloodied altars — God needs nothing humans could give. Tertullian turns the same rule against Marcion: the Creator, not a new stranger god, is the one prayed to and adored. The only wrinkle inside the agreement is practice: Victorinus already keeps Friday station and fast, Sabbath carrying-over, and Lord's-day bread with thanksgiving, while Commodian orders conduct before God's holy things — assembly discipline beside the apologists' 'no temples, no altars.'

title: The Creator's image, able to fail
body: Both excerpts are Tertullian against Marcion: man is the Creator's image, so only the Creator's Christ can be his head — a stranger god has no rights over him. Yet the image need not match its truth at every point: breath, the image of spirit, can sin without God's Spirit sinning. Creation and fallenness hold together here; no later break is staged.

title: A foretold mission, contested sender
body: Tertullian reads the mission straight out of the prophets: timely feet on the mountains, sound gone out into all the earth, twelve apostles figured in Elim's springs and seventy in its palms. The fight is over whose mission it is — Marcion's stranger god, or the Creator whose Scripture the apostles were filling even as they suffered.

title: Priority decides: churches against the late emender
body: The whole case turns on time: what is earlier is truer, what is from the beginning is from the apostles, and what the apostles handed down stands sacrosanct in the apostles' churches — Corinth, Galatia, Philippi, Rome. Marcion, first appearing under Antoninus with an authorless, cut-down Luke, claims to restore what the apostles corrupted; Tertullian answers that the worldwide gospel predates him by a century and needs no Pontic emender.

title: A written passion, a summed-up beginning
body: Tertullian binds atonement to prophecy on both ends: the suffering servant of Isaiah — led as a sheep, taking our weaknesses — and Paul's recapitulation of all things in Christ, which can only belong to the God who owns the beginning. A workless stranger god has no beginning to sum up and no written passion to fulfill; Marcion's phantom cannot own either scene.

title: Light offered, eyes covered
body: Lactantius opens Book 5 with a plea, not a proof: do not condemn before hearing the whole case — yet men shout truth down and cover their eyes lest they see the light. Evil, on his account, needs no evil god to explain it: greed burst from contempt of the true majesty, custom hardened into habit, and justice left dragging truth with her. The rupture here is internal to the reader — offered light refused.

title: Soul escape or flesh rising
body: Two hopes collide. Marcion promises a celestial-only kingdom and salvation for the soul alone; Tertullian answers that the Creator is merciful even to the dead — restoring what wrath removed, refreshing the faithful in Abraham's bosom — and that Paul's whole chain in 1 Corinthians 15, from baptism for the dead to 'with what body,' binds hope to the flesh's rising. The resurrection always denied is the resurrection of the body.

title: Diversity confessed, second god denied
body: Marcion's Antitheses make diversity of law and gospel prove two gods; Tertullian concedes the diversity and denies the inference. The talion restrains violence, food laws train continence, the sabbath bars human works but not divine — and the new law from Zion, the new wine, the fulfilled fishers' prophecy, Moses and Elijah beside Christ on the mount, all show the Creator arranging and foretelling his own newness. One God disposed both the old burden and the gospel liberty.

title: Eternal care against a worldless stranger
body: Providence is proved by works: the eternal goodness that willed to be known, ravens fed and lilies clothed, anxious care forbidden because the Father already supplies. Against this Tertullian sets Marcion's god — revealed late under Tiberius, his substance under Severus found to be nothing, multiplying into maker, place, and matter, too late to check the Creator and too hasty before his Christ. A god with no world shows no care.

title: Fed by God, testifying to a Judge
body: One excerpt, double-edged: the disciples carry nothing because the Creator feeds ravens and clothes flowers and pays the threshing ox — and they shake dust for a testimony, which only a coming Judge makes sense. Bagless mission and threatened judgment both point the same way, back to the God of the prophets.

title: Many motives, one Christ announced
body: Paul lists the motives — boldness, envy, contention, good will, love, rivalry, even pretence — and Tertullian's point is what Paul does not tax: the preaching itself. Causes of minds vary; the sacrament's rule does not. One Christ is announced whether from pretext or from truth, and Marcion cannot split a second Christ out of missionary rivalry that Paul already relativized.

title: Truly born, truly suffered
body: Ignatius (c. 110) is the anchor: truly born of a virgin, truly suffered, still possessed of flesh after the resurrection — and those who say He only seemed to suffer only seem to be Christians. Irenaeus and Novatian stand on the same line a century later. The break is with the docetists, not between the fathers; no writer in this set softens the flesh.

title: Dead matter, live demons
body: Justin, Diognetus, Athenagoras, and Theophilus agree the images are soulless dead matter of recent date — yet Athenagoras adds that demons work through them, so the polemic is not mere rationalism. Athenagoras also denies many gods from the beginning: one uncreated Maker. The break falls against both the idol-maker and the polytheist, not within the Christian writers.

title: Prophets first, philosophy as servant
body: Tertullian and Clement both argue from the prophets and Israel's older writings — fulfilled prophecy is the shared proof. Clement alone gives Greek philosophy a real but qualified office: it can prepare the mind, yet the philosophers name God without knowing Him. The break is between prophecy's certainty and philosophy's junior, preparatory role.

title: Show the roll
body: Irenaeus names the Roman roll — Linus, Anacletus, Clement — and Tertullian turns it into a challenge: let rival churches produce their original records from those Christ appointed. Unauthorized meetings have no such claim, both agree. The break is evidential: a succession you can list versus assemblies you cannot.

title: Summing up Adam
body: This set is Irenaeus-heavy: the Son recapitulates Adam's ancient fashioning, gives soul for soul and flesh for flesh, and crushes the serpent who led us captive — with Melito, Tertullian, Novatian, and Commodian furnishing neighboring victory and exchange language. No writer here offers a rival account of the mechanism. The break is against the heretical denials Irenaeus says perish before this account, not an internal split.

title: Good Maker, free creature
body: Justin denies God needs material offerings; Athenagoras and Theophilus describe Him as uncreated, eternal, and known through His works and providence. Irenaeus holds providence together with liberty: man was made a free agent from the beginning. The break is against both the gift-needing god of the cults and any providence that cancels choice.

title: Taught, then washed
body: Justin requires persuasion and teaching before the water; Barnabas and Hermas then read the washing itself as the turn — sins go down, fruit and the seal of the kingdom come up. Clement crowns it: to be regenerated and illuminated is to know God. The break is sequential, not contested: faith first, then a water that truly regenerates.

title: One public rule
body: Irenaeus carries the verdicts here: the dispersed church holds one faith received from the apostles, the apostolic Gospel handed down in the Scriptures — with Tertullian, Cyprian, and Eusebius supplying neighboring excerpts. Against the heretics he denies the escape hatch: confuted from the Scriptures, they appeal to a hidden tradition instead. The break is public rule versus secret Gnosis.

title: Choice, not fate
body: Tatian puts Christians above fate and its demon lawgivers; Justin insists each succeeds or sins by deliberate choice, God having made angels and men self-determining. Justin and Dionysius of Alexandria alike deny the rival cosmologies — Stoic necessity and Epicurean atoms colliding at random. The break is total: foreknowledge judges free choosers; fate and chance explain nothing.

title: Triad without two Gods
body: From the Didache through Justin and Athenagoras to Novatian, Father, Son, and Spirit are named and worshipped together, and Novatian affirms the Son is not the Father. The same Novatian denies the inference his critics feared: Scripture does not set forth two Gods. The break is the tightrope itself — distinction without division — held unanimously across 120–250.

title: Waiting, not yet above
body: Irenaeus affirms the disciples' souls wait in the invisible, allotted place until the resurrection and expressly denies that the just pass immediately above the heavens; Tertullian fills in Hades with Lazarus and the rich man. Irenaeus's graded mansions — heaven, paradise, the city — come after the end, not at death. The break is against immediate ascent, not between these two writers.

title: Flee, and do not rend
body: Didache, Ignatius, and Tertullian agree on flight from strange doctrine — poison in sweet wine — while Irenaeus and Cyprian treat schism as cutting the body and rending the Lord's garment. Cyprian's hard corollary denies heretic baptism: he who is without cannot give the Spirit. The break sharpens over time from avoidance to invalidity.

title: Types yes, shadows no
body: Barnabas, Justin, and Tertullian read the Old Testament as types of Christ — food laws, Passover lamb, the predicted cross. Irenaeus denies the gnostic inversion that this world is a shadow of a bodiless order above, and Clement's philosophy-as-preparation stays qualified. The break: typology that honors the Creator's history versus allegory that dissolves it.

title: The Word truly came in flesh
body: Barnabas, Ignatius, Justin, and Diognetus affirm the Word truly became flesh — born, eating and drinking, crucified — and Ignatius denies appearance-only outright. Justin presses the point against pagan parallels: Christ is the proper Son, not another son of Jupiter. No writer in this set wavers; the break is wholly against the seemers.

title: Watch — He comes to judge
body: The Didache's watchfulness (you know not the hour) runs through Irenaeus to fulfilment after Antichrist and the resurrection. Justin defends eternal fire against those who call it a bugbear. The break is against minimizing the judgment, not between the writers, who hold coming and fire together.

title: The Lord's Day, not the Sabbath
body: The Didache commands the set prayer; Ignatius moves the assembly from Sabbath observance to the Lord's Day, on which our life sprang up again. Justin names it plainly: the day called Sunday. The break is calendrical and unanimous in this set — new day, commanded prayer, no return to the old Sabbath.

title: Even enemies — the Creator's own command
body: Didache and Barnabas root the way of life in love of God and neighbor, and Justin with Athenagoras extends it to enemies: pray for persecutors, love those who hate you. Tertullian's edge is anti-Marcionite — love your enemies is the Creator's old injunction, not a new god's novelty. No break appears in this set; the command only widens.

title: Argue from the Seventy
body: Justin anchors apologetic argument in the Seventy's Greek and refuses the move he sees in contemporary Jewish teachers: discarding the Seventy to frame another text. Clement retells the Ptolemy translation story as shared ground. The break is textual authority — the church's Greek Bible stands, and later corrections of it are denied.

title: Soldiers longing for battle, not pain
body: Tertullian, Minucius Felix, and the Passion of Perpetua line up on martyrdom as a soldier's battle for God — glorious, watched by God, crowned with eternal life. The break is the pagan taunt preserved in Apology 50: if Christians want to suffer, why complain of persecution. Tertullian denies the charge while holding the confession: the soldier longs for the war's glory and spoil, not for pain itself.

title: One God of both covenants
body: Barnabas, Irenaeus, and Tertullian all affirm one God behind both testaments, with the new covenant coming from the same God as the old; Marcion's split of law and gospel into two gods is denied at every turn. The internal edge is Barnabas, whose verdict is qualified: the covenant sworn to the fathers now belongs to Christians because Israel proved unworthy to receive it. So the rupture runs two ways — Marcion sundered outwardly, Barnabas pressing supersession from inside the one-God camp.

title: With the bishop or outside the mother
body: Ignatius (c. 110) makes unity with the bishop the mark of belonging to God, and Cyprian (251–255) extends the line into a full doctrine: the episcopate is one and undivided, and remission of sins is granted in the Church alone. Schismatics who follow a divider inherit nothing; heretics without altar or church cannot baptize or anoint. The qualified verdicts leave the door open only one way — return by repentance into the one Mother.

title: One maker from nothing
body: Hermas, Athenagoras, and Tatian affirm one God who made all things, Hermas adding 'out of nothing,' while Justin denies Marcion's preaching of another god besides the Creator. The verdicts are unanimous across 100–177 with no internal dissent in this seed. The break is the Marcionite second god — the one-maker confession exists here largely as its refutation.

title: Truly suffered, risen in flesh
body: Barnabas and Ignatius affirm that Christ truly suffered, died, and rose; Ignatius adds that he rose still possessed of flesh, eating and drinking, to be handled and not mistaken for a spirit. The docetic claim that he only seemed to suffer is denied outright. The verdict base is narrow — two writers, c. 100–110 — but fully agreed, with the rupture drawn against seeming-only Christology.

title: This flesh rises, same identity
body: Ignatius, Justin, Tatian, Athenagoras, Irenaeus, Theophilus, Tertullian, and Minucius Felix affirm that this flesh rises, the same identity that died receiving the same body. Soul-only recompense is denied three ways: Athenagoras argues laws were given to the whole man, Tertullian answers those who sever resurrection from flesh, and Minucius refuses Pythagorean transmigration as misrepresentation. Origen affirms that what died was a body while opening the harder question of what kind of body stands at judgment.

title: Deeds judged, death not the end
body: The Didache, Justin, Athenagoras, Minucius Felix, and Arnobius affirm that acts — not fate, birth-chart, or status — are judged, with the living and the dead facing a final reckoning. Lactantius denies the death-ends-all persuasion: if we are nothing after death, virtue looks foolish and justice collapses. The break is between accountability and its dissolvers, whether fatalism or annihilation.

title: Ransom by the Son's blood
body: Barnabas, Diognetus, Ignatius, Hippolytus, and Methodius affirm rescue by the incarnate Son's blood, salvation located in Christ alone — the holy for the lawless, the immortal for the mortal. Diognetus explicitly denies the rival claim that we were saved because we were already righteous. There is no dissent in this seed; the only rupture marked is worth-based rescue, refused.

title: Prophetic Spirit wrote; poets did not
body: Justin and Athenagoras affirm that the prophetic Spirit published the Scriptures beforehand through the prophets, and Irenaeus adds the apostolic half: the Gospel handed down in writing as ground and pillar of faith. Theophilus denies poets and philosophers equal standing — fables and contradictions, not the exhibition of God. The break sets Spirit-moved prophecy and apostolic writing against pagan letters on one side and, by implication, any gospel not handed down in the Scriptures.

title: Marriage honored, remarriage contested
body: Didache, Barnabas, Hermas, and Athenagoras unite in forbidding fornication and adultery, while Hermas and Clement affirm marriage as good — Hermas with 'remember your own wife,' Clement with careful qualifications of suitable person, time, and manner. The break is Tertullian's Montanist-era rigor refusing second marriage, set between heretics who abolish marriage and 'psychics' who accumulate it. Remarriage is the one claim in this topic where the verdicts split into affirm and qualified rather than standing unanimous.

title: Water and Spirit together
body: Didache, Justin, and Clement affirm triadic baptism as regeneration and new birth, and Tertullian joins the Spirit to the water — hovering at creation, invoked with the laying on of hands. Against claims that faith without baptism suffices, Tertullian denies flatly: after the nativity, passion, and resurrection, bare faith has been clothed with the sealing sacrament, and without baptism salvation is attainable by none. The rupture is bare-faith sufficiency versus water-and-Spirit necessity.

title: The Word spoke; try the spirits
body: Justin and Athenagoras affirm that the Divine Word and Spirit spoke in the prophets — sometimes as God, sometimes as Christ, sometimes as the people answering — and deny that the prophets spoke only their own words. Hermas supplies the testing rule this high doctrine requires: two kinds of spirit, and prophets tried by their works, with the empty soothsayer answering doubters according to their wishes. The break is true Spirit-moved prophecy against false, wish-fed oracles.

title: Indwelling Spirit, grieved by vice
body: Hermas, Irenaeus, and Barnabas affirm that the Holy Spirit dwells in the faithful and makes holy — Barnabas picturing the heart as temple, Irenaeus the indwelling earnest tending toward incorruption. Hermas adds the rupture within the doctrine: anger, sadness, and vice straiten, darken, and grieve the tender Spirit until He seeks to depart, while patience keeps Him pure. No writer here dissents; the break is moral, drawn inside each believer's household.

title: God and perfect man, one subject
body: Ignatius, Diognetus, Melito, Irenaeus, and Novatian affirm that the same one is God and a perfect human being — Melito naming two substances confirmed by signs and by the hidden years of flesh. Novatian denies both rival reductions: man only and alone, and God without true flesh. The rupture is three-cornered, with the twofold confession holding the center against adoptionist thinning on one side and fleshless divinity on the other.

title: Life or death, no third way
body: Didache, Barnabas, Hermas, and Commodian affirm the two ways without exception — life and death, light and darkness, righteousness and wickedness, with no third path offered. Didache and Barnabas define the way of life as love of God and neighbor; Hermas internalizes the pair as two angels known by their works in the heart. This is the most unanimous topic in the set: the only break is the choice itself.

title: Born of a virgin, not of adultery
body: Ignatius (three passages) and Justin affirm Christ born of a virgin as Isaiah foretold — of David's seed according to the flesh, conceived without intercourse. Origen denies the rival account head-on, answering Celsus's Jew and the Panthera adultery slander as an invention meant to overturn the miraculous conception. The break pits Isaiah-fulfillment confession against pagan-Jewish polemic of ordinary or illicit generation.

title: No abiding city; wealth for alms
body: Hermas, Barnabas, Tertullian, Cyprian, and Clement affirm that wealth exists for alms and the poor — Clement urging riches partaken rationally and bestowed lovingly, Tertullian exhibiting the common fund as Christianity's positive good. Hermas frames the rupture: this is a strange land with no abiding city, so piling lands and houses is folly, while rich and poor need each other as elm and vine. The break is treasure in heaven against settling here as if home.
